capabilities.target: Chat reply delivered to the authenticated requester
Jira tickets, including those filed by customers

inputs.source: Employee question via SSO-authenticated chat session
Jira tickets filed by customers, via planned Jira MCP connector

instructions.note: The only control against leaking confidential content is a prompt instruction ('Never paste secrets or credentials into answers'); there is no structural data-loss-prevention check, and the instruction only covers credentials/secrets, not confidential document content generally. This gap becomes materially more important once an egress-capable tool (web.fetch) exists.

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never paste secrets or credentials into answers
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to withhold secrets; a more capable or adversarially prompted model can be argued into including them, and it only addresses credentials, not confidential business content generally.

controls.name: Only engineers can write to design docs
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced by the document system's write ACL, not by the agent or model; a stronger model cannot write to the docs store regardless of behavior.

controls.name: Chat replies bound to the authenticated requester; client does not render images or fetch links
controls.decay_rationale: The reply destination is fixed by the session's authenticated identity, not chosen by the model, and the client has no link/image rendering channel for covert egress. Does not decay with model capability.

controls.name: No network egress capability exists today
controls.decay_rationale: No tool or credential in the current design can reach the network, so no model behavior can exfiltrate data externally. This control is defeated the moment an egress-capable tool such as web.fetch is added (new_tool trigger).

controls.name: docs.search credential is read-only
controls.decay_rationale: Prevents the agent from writing or deleting design docs regardless of model behavior, but does not restrict reading confidential content, so it does not mitigate confidentiality exfiltration risk.

controls.name: Egress allowlist restricting web.fetch to fixed public reference domains, with no model-controlled query parameters
controls.decay_rationale: If destinations are a fixed allowlist excluding attacker-writable endpoints and the agent cannot pass document content as query parameters, this would sever the exfiltration path regardless of model behavior. Not yet designed.

controls.name: Provenance tagging and segregation of customer-authored Jira ticket content from trusted instructions and query construction
controls.decay_rationale: If enforced at the ingestion layer rather than by model self-discipline, ticket content could never be treated as an instruction or used to parameterize docs_search/web_fetch calls. Not yet designed.

controls.name: Human approval gate on web.fetch calls, with raw-action review of destination and payload
controls.decay_rationale: A raw-action approval gate on outbound web.fetch calls would cap residual risk regardless of model capability, but no such gate exists in the design today.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1), forecast: customer-filed Jira tickets could steer docs.search and exfiltrate confidential design docs via planned web.fetch

attack_path.note: Customer-authored ticket content enters the agent's context via the planned Jira MCP connector (untrusted source).
Planned tool call retrieves ticket content, including customer-authored text, into context.
Agent reads confidential engineering design docs, potentially with query terms or follow-on instructions shaped by the untrusted ticket content.
Planned tool with network egress; a crafted URL or query parameter could carry confidential document content to an attacker-controlled destination.

forecast.watch_signal: web.fetch appears in the tool manifest, or a Jira MCP server entry appears in the MCP client config / tools list; either connector's enabled flag flips in deployment config.

evidence.observation: 'There is no network egress today. The credential is read only.' This is the control that keeps the current design's residual risk low.

'Roadmap for next sprint: add a web.fetch tool so answers can include public references, and connect a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers.' Adds an egress-capable tool and an untrusted content source in the same change.

The system prompt instructs the agent to use docs.search and cite sources, and not to paste secrets, but has no rule for treating ticket content as untrusted or constraining what web.fetch may be called with.

recommendations.action: Before enabling web.fetch, restrict it to a fixed allowlist of reference domains and disallow passing document content or model-chosen query parameters in the request, so confidential text cannot be smuggled out through the URL.

Tag content ingested from the Jira connector as untrusted at the point of ingestion, and block it from being used to construct docs.search queries or web.fetch arguments without passing through an injection-aware check.
Until the allowlist above exists, require a raw-action human approval gate on any web.fetch call whose arguments were influenced by Jira-sourced content.

governance_refs.note: Emergent risk tracked ahead of the connector being built.

rating.rationale: No present-horizon finding reaches above low: docs.search is read-only and confidential-doc content only ever flows back to the same SSO-authenticated requester, with no network egress capability in today's design (ctl.no_network_egress and ctl.destination_binding both sever any path to an external destination). The roadmap combination of a planned web.fetch tool (egress) and a planned Jira MCP connector (an untrusted, customer-authored input) reopens the lethal trifecta: once the new_tool/new_mcp_server triggers fire, ctl.no_network_egress is defeated and no other declared control covers confidentiality loss through web.fetch, so the forecast rises to critical. The single highest-leverage fix is to implement the recommended structural, independent egress allowlist on web.fetch (ctl.web_fetch_egress_allowlist) before it ships; its absence is the control decay driving the forecast.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.
No MCP config or tool manifest was provided for docs.search; its scope is inferred from the runtime notes, so confidence on current capabilities is medium.

The planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP connector are described only as roadmap items with no manifest, schema, or access-control design; the forecast finding's specifics (allowlist, credential scope, auth) are inferred from typical implementations of such features, not from provided specifications.
